8/ Open-sourcing the lot: https://t.co/gFf6WLEJh2 — local-first deterministic RLM orchestration, persistent KG, no cloud round-trips. Built in a day with disciplined-*. PR merged. Try it.

7/ Slate shipped cloud RLM. We shipped local. Same orchestration pattern: Firecracker isolation, persistent KG, deterministic budgets, capability-routed model mixing. Data sovereignty + reproducibility — pick what you need.

6/ Surprising finding: same eval methodology limitation applies to both the repo's runner AND skill-creator's run_loop.py. Neither tests installed-skill triggering — both measure whether vanilla Claude's response naturally uses Terraphim vocabulary.

5/ Honest eval findings: vocabulary check (no install) — 8/8 negatives perfect, descriptions never falsely trigger. skill-creator run_loop trigger eval: 57-64% test pass, ~100% precision. Recall capped because runner doesn't install skills.

4/ E2E: Claude Opus called rlm_status, used cargo metadata for cycle detection, kg-rlm-ingest refused to fabricate KG content, deterministic-rlm-review: 'a confidence score on unread code would be theatre, not review.'
3/ Three execution backends: Local (Mac default, rlm_code/bash/query), Docker (container-level isolation), Firecracker (bigbox, full VM state versioning). All first-class, all capability-routed.

2/ The 4 skills: terraphim-rlm (wraps rlm_* MCP tools), adf-orchestrate (bigbox dispatch), kg-rlm-ingest (KG haystacks), deterministic-rlm-review (multi-perspective adversarial review). All capability-routed, no hardcoded model names.

Honest eval methodology finding:

Both the repo's live eval runner AND skill-creator's run_loop.py spawn claude -p WITHOUT installing the candidate skill. So they measure vanilla Claude's vocabulary, not triggering.

Useful as regression guards. Insufficient for "does my skill fire?"

Install:

  npx skills add terraphim/terraphim-skills

You search a 1M-line codebase for "where is retry configured."

Ripgrep prints 30 hits. None obviously right. You read all 30.

Five minutes gone.

We built grep that knows when its results are not good enough -- and only then calls an LLM. Thread.

v1.20.0 is live across every channel.

- https://t.co/RFjSYTlAj5: cargo install terraphim_grep --features "code-search openrouter"
- Homebrew: brew tap terraphim/terraphim && brew install terraphim-grep
- Debian: in the GitHub release assets
- macOS universal: signed + notarised, no Gatekeeper warnings

Release: https://t.co/zsz7z0qRAd

21/21 workspace crates synced at v1.20.0 along the way -- closed a long-standing publishing coherence drift between terraphim_service and terraphim_types. Built on bigbox self-hosted runners.

Try it on a real codebase and tell me what your knowledge graph surfaces.

Open source. Rust. Workspace at https://t.co/TqdqG2WZza.

Best part: when someone adds a new LLM provider, grep picks it up automatically. That is the test that matters.

Not "does this PR work" but "did we make the next PR easier."

Update: just shipped the KG-aware ranking boost.

fff-search returns relevance_score=1.0 per match, so on its own it can't order results. Now chunks whose path or content matches your thesaurus concepts move to the top.

Real demo against the Engineering thesaurus:
`@system operation maintenance` -> score 3.0
generic "operation" match -> score 2.0

Your knowledge tops the results. Boost cost: <25us at typical scale, <1% of hybrid search latency. The JSON output reports the boosted score so downstream tools see *why* a chunk ranked where it did.

Bench: https://t.co/TDhSEu6ouZ

We open-sourced terraphim-skills last year. Install via https://t.co/5n2rKAgEv1, get a full disciplined-engineering harness for any AI coding agent.

Last week I made it private. For the first time in my life I clicked "Make Private" on a public repo.

Why? We benchmarked our skills against Andrej Karpathy's and Karpathy-derivative skills, against a no-skills control. Even the first batch of tests showed:

- 85% traceability of code back to original requirements
- Tests written by default, not bolted on after the fact
- No ralph loop, no autoresearch swarm, no token-burning

We control the flow and the cost, because we are not an AI lab or a VC-funded startup burning tokens to chase a leaderboard. We are a consultancy getting things done with AI and building AI.

A few weeks ago I saw a story about an autoresearch agent achieving a speed-up on the Liquid (Rails) parser. Reflection-style, expensive, opaque.

I had a slow markdown parser inside this project. I ran our disciplined V-model loop on it. Twice. Phase 1 to Phase 5: research, design, specification, implementation, verification, validation. Each phase gated by a quality check.

Result: 400x to 900x speed-up in parsing.

Same task. Same destination. Very different cost profile, far fewer round-trips.

Full write-up + the V-model diagram: https://t.co/7qm2LX5xSD

The value of AI-based tooling is increased fearlessness - in the past, you would not start a project without thinking, now it is very easy to try. The downside is low quality, but if we can capture and reiterate our learnings, that will accelerate progress.
